To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the specific alterations induced during tumor progression can determine both the tumor response and the specific susceptibilities to conventional chemotherapy, as well as to specific targeted agents; (ii) this is exemplified by the combined status of the two most commonly mutated tumor suppressors, p53 and ATM, which determines the response to genotoxic chemotherapy and the specific vulnerabilities to DNA-PK inhibition

the combined status of the tumor suppressors ATM and p53 is predictive of the tumor response to DNA-damagin chemotherapeutic agents, and that the combined status can also be used to identify specific tumor susceptibilities to targeted therapeutics.
the combined status of the ATM and p53 pathways is predictive of tumor response to genotoxic chemotherapy and can identify tumors that are susceptible to targeted therapies that inhibit DNA-PKcs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how tumor suppressor networks are altered in tumors and how these alterations can influence the response of these tumors to therapy.
the identification of molecular targets that are critical for the survival of cancer cells.
the development of novel therapies that exploit tumor-specific vulnerabilities to improve the clinical efficacy of cancer therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combined status of p53 and ATM is a critical factor that can predict the clinical response of a tumor to DNA-damagin chemotherapy.

the combined status of p53 and ATM can predict the chemoresistance of tumors to DNA-damage-inducing chemotherapy, and that this chemosensitizing strategy can be exploited to resensitize chemoresistant tumors to DNA-damping chemotherapy by targeting DNA-PKcs.
the specific set of genetic alterations induced during tumor evolution determines both the response of tumors and their specific susceptibilities to conventional and targeted therapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combined status of two commonly mutated tumor-suppressor networks (ATM and p53) can predict chemotherapeutic response in a tumor type-specific fashion, and the identification of tumor vulnerabilities that arise in the context of ATM deficiency can be used to resensitize tumors to DNA-damage-inducing therapies.
in p53-mutant cancers, ATM inhibition sensitizes tumors to genotoxic chemotherapy, whereas in p53 wild-type cancers, ATM inhibition actually protects from genotoxic chemotherapy.

the combined status of p53 and ATM is a strong predictor of the tumor response to genotoxic therapies and that tumors with a defective ATM pathway are particularly vulnerable to suppression of DNA-Pkcs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combined status of specific tumor suppressors can help to predict chemotherapeutic response, and that the mechanisms used by tumors to evade early neoplastic checks ultimately determine the response to genotoxic therapy.
the combined status of tumor suppressors is critical to determine the response of tumors not only to conventional chemotherapies but also to targeted agents.

the response of tumors with specific genetic alterations to conventional chemotherapeutic agents is determined by the specific set of tumor suppressor alterations that have accumulated during tumor development.
